warmup.q: A Jetty 12 server uses its default thread pool. A handler that extends Handler.Abstract (so it declares itself blocking) calls a 300 ms JDBC query. Which thread usually runs it?
options: A worker thread taken from the pool's queue, like Tomcat does for every request
The selector thread that read the request, while a spare reserved thread takes over the selecting
A virtual thread, because Jetty 12 enables them by default
The acceptor thread that accepted the connection
warmup.why: Jetty's adaptive execution strategy prefers to run a task on the thread that produced it, while its data is still in that CPU's cache. For a blocking task it does that only when a reserved thread is free to take over selecting, the Execute-Produce-Consume mode. The demo in this lesson shows epcRunTask in the handler's stack. Virtual threads are off unless you configure them.

sections.h: A Jetty server is connectors, handlers and one thread pool
sections.html:
Jetty's documentation describes a Server as the component that links a collection of Connectors and a collection of Handlers, with threads from one ThreadPool doing all the work. Every thread you'll see in this lesson comes from that one pool.

The connector you'll use is the ServerConnector. It has two kinds of threads. Acceptors (one by default) call accept() and hand each new socket on. A SelectorManager owns several ManagedSelectors, and each ManagedSelector is one thread running a java.nio Selector: the select loop from lesson 2, so epoll on Linux. By default there are max(1, min(cpus / 2, maxThreads / 16)) selectors, and the docs give a rule of thumb that one selector manages 1,000 to 5,000 sockets. Inside, each socket becomes an EndPoint that moves bytes and a Connection that parses a protocol (HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, WebSocket).

Java
Server server = new Server(new QueuedThreadPool());   // one pool for everything
ServerConnector connector = new ServerConnector(server);
connector.setHost("127.0.0.1");
connector.setPort(8080);
server.addConnector(connector);
server.setHandler(new LedgerHandler(300));
server.start();
Kotlin
val server = Server(QueuedThreadPool())                // one pool for everything
val connector = ServerConnector(server).apply { host = "127.0.0.1"; port = 8080 }
server.addConnector(connector)
server.handler = LedgerHandler(300)
server.start()

The default pool is a QueuedThreadPool with at least 8 and at most 200 threads. The connector leases some of them for good: this section's demo, on 4 CPUs, shows 1 acceptor, 2 selectors and 3 leased threads. The pool must have room for those plus at least one thread for requests, and the docs suggest sizing maxThreads as the leased threads plus the threads you want for handlers.

Two pool rules surprise people. The pool's queue must be unbounded. Jetty sometimes needs to run its own tasks to make progress (HTTP/2, for example, must write in order to read), and the docs warn that a rejected task can make the server grind to a halt. Limit load with a QoS handler instead. And a platform thread costs about 1 MiB of native memory, so 200 threads is a real number.

code.title: JettyThreadsDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.nio.l07; import org.eclipse.jetty.io.Content; import org.eclipse.jetty.server.Handler; import org.eclipse.jetty.server.Request; import org.eclipse.jetty.server.Response; import org.eclipse.jetty.server.Server; import org.eclipse.jetty.server.ServerConnector; import org.eclipse.jetty.util.Callback; import org.eclipse.jetty.util.VirtualThreads; import org.eclipse.jetty.util.thread.QueuedThreadPool; import org.eclipse.jetty.util.thread.ThreadPool; import java.net.URI; import java.net.http.HttpClient; import java.net.http.HttpRequest; import java.net.http.HttpResponse; /** What does a default Jetty 12 server start, and which thread runs a blocking vs a non-blocking handler? */ public class JettyThreadsDemo { static final HttpClient CLIENT = HttpClient.newBuilder().proxy(HttpClient.Builder.NO_PROXY).build(); static String where() { Thread t = Thread.currentThread(); return t.getName() + " virtual=" + t.isVirtual(); } static class Blocking extends Handler.Abstract { // declares BLOCKING @Override public boolean handle(Request req, Response res, Callback cb) { Content.Sink.write(res, true, where(), cb); return true; } } static class NonBlocking extends Handler.Abstract.NonBlocking { // declares NON_BLOCKING @Override public boolean handle(Request req, Response res, Callback cb) { Content.Sink.write(res, true, where(), cb); return true; } } static Server start(ThreadPool pool, Handler handler) throws Exception { Server server = new Server(pool); ServerConnector connector = new ServerConnector(server); connector.setHost("127.0.0.1"); connector.setPort(0); server.addConnector(connector); server.setHandler(handler); server.start(); return server; } static String get(Server server) throws Exception { int port = ((ServerConnector) server.getConnectors()[0]).getLocalPort(); return CLIENT.send(HttpRequest.newBuilder(URI.create("http://127.0.0.1:" + port + "/")).build(), HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()).body(); } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { QueuedThreadPool defaults = new QueuedThreadPool(); Server server = start(defaults, new Blocking()); ServerConnector c = (ServerConnector) server.getConnectors()[0]; System.out.println("cpus=" + Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors() + " acceptors=" + c.getAcceptors() + " selectors=" + c.getSelectorManager().getSelectorCount()); System.out.println("QueuedThreadPool min=" + defaults.getMinThreads() + " max=" + defaults.getMaxThreads() + " started=" + defaults.getThreads() + " leased=" + defaults.getLeasedThreads()); System.out.println("[platform pool] BLOCKING handler -> " + get(server)); server.stop(); server = start(new QueuedThreadPool(), new NonBlocking()); System.out.println("[platform pool] NON_BLOCKING handler -> " + get(server)); server.stop(); for (boolean blocking : new boolean[] {true, false}) { QueuedThreadPool pool = new QueuedThreadPool(); pool.setVirtualThreadsExecutor(VirtualThreads.getNamedVirtualThreadsExecutor("jetty-vt-")); server = start(pool, blocking ? new Blocking() : new NonBlocking()); System.out.println("[pool + virtual threads] " + (blocking ? "BLOCKING handler -> " : "NON_BLOCKING handler -> ") + get(server)); server.stop(); } } }

port = 0 }) this.handler = handler start() } private fun get(server: Server): String { val port = (server.connectors[0] as ServerConnector).localPort return client.send(HttpRequest.newBuilder(URI.create("http://127.0.0.1:$port/")).build(), HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()).body() } fun main() { val defaults = QueuedThreadPool() var server = startServer(defaults, KtBlocking()) val c = server.connectors[0] as ServerConnector println("cpus=${Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors()} acceptors=${c.acceptors} selectors=${c.selectorManager.selectorCount}") println("QueuedThreadPool min=${defaults.minThreads} max=${defaults.maxThreads} started=${defaults.threads} leased=${defaults.leasedThreads}") println("[platform pool] BLOCKING handler -> ${get(server)}") server.stop() server = startServer(QueuedThreadPool(), KtNonBlocking()) println("[platform pool] NON_BLOCKING handler -> ${get(server)}") server.stop() for (blocking in listOf(true, false)) { val pool = QueuedThreadPool() pool.virtualThreadsExecutor = VirtualThreads.getNamedVirtualThreadsExecutor("jetty-vt-") server = startServer(pool, if (blocking) KtBlocking() else KtNonBlocking()) println("[pool + virtual threads] ${if (blocking) "BLOCKING handler -> " else "NON_BLOCKING handler -> "}${get(server)}") server.stop() } }

try.expect: On 4 CPUs: acceptors=1 selectors=2 and QueuedThreadPool min=8 max=200 started=8 leased=3 (one acceptor, two selectors). With a 12-thread pool the formula gives max(1, min(2, 12 / 16 = 0)) = 1 selector. Jetty also logs a few INFO lines when servers start and stop.

sections.h: The core Handler API is asynchronous
sections.html:
Jetty 12 rewrote the API at its center. In Jetty 11 a handler had a blocking signature built on Servlet types. In Jetty 12 it is boolean handle(Request request, Response response, Callback callback), and the migration guide spells out the new contract: return true to say you handled the request, and then complete the Callback, by succeeding or failing it, possibly long after handle has returned. Return false and Jetty moves on; with no other handler, the client gets a 404.

A blocking handler is the simple case: do the work, write the response with Content.Sink.write(response, true, text, callback), which completes the callback once the bytes are written, and return true. A non-blocking handler reads the body without waiting for it:

Java
public class EchoHandler extends Handler.Abstract.NonBlocking {
    @Override
    public boolean handle(Request request, Response response, Callback callback) {
        Content.Source.asStringAsync(request, UTF_8).whenComplete((body, failure) -> {
            if (failure != null) {
                Response.writeError(request, response, callback, failure);
                return;
            }
            Content.Sink.write(response, true, "echo: " + body, callback);   // completes the callback
        });
        return true;   // "I took this request"; the response finishes later
    }
}
Kotlin
class EchoHandler : Handler.Abstract.NonBlocking() {
    override fun handle(request: Request, response: Response, callback: Callback): Boolean {
        Content.Source.asStringAsync(request, UTF_8).whenComplete { body, failure ->
            if (failure != null) {
                Response.writeError(request, response, callback, failure)
            } else {
                Content.Sink.write(response, true, "echo: $body", callback)  // completes the callback
            }
        }
        return true   // "I took this request"; the response finishes later
    }
}

The request body is a Content.Source: you read it in Content.Chunks, which are slices of Jetty's network buffers, passed up without copying. The rule echoes Netty's reference counting from lesson 4: every chunk you read() must be released, except failure chunks, and a source must be read to the end or failed, or Jetty can leak its buffers. Helpers such as asStringAsync do the reading and releasing for you.

The superclass is a declaration. Handler.Abstract says "I may block" (InvocationType.BLOCKING). Handler.Abstract.NonBlocking says "I never block", and Jetty uses that promise to pick a thread, as the next section shows.

The Servlet API still exists, as a layer on top of this core. Jetty 12 ships it in separate environments named after Jakarta EE versions: ee8, ee9, ee10, and since 12.1 ee11, which brings Servlet 6.1. The docs list the core API's strengths as simple, minimal and asynchronous, with low overhead because you only configure what you use.

try.title: Break the handler contract
steps: In JettyThreadsDemo, change the Blocking handler's body to just return false; (delete the Content.Sink.write line). Predict what the first GET prints.
Put it back. Now think it through without running it: what does a client see if a handler returns true and never completes the callback?
try.expect: With return false the request finds no handler and Jetty answers with a 404 page, which the demo prints as the body. A handler that returns true and never completes the callback leaves the request open: the client waits until its own timeout or Jetty's idle timeout ends the connection. Returning true is a promise to finish the response exactly once.

sections.h: One strategy, three modes: who runs your handler
sections.html:
When a selector finds a readable socket, it produces a task: "run this connection's onFillable", which parses the request and calls your handler. Jetty's AdaptiveExecutionStrategy then decides which thread consumes that task, and it has three main modes, named in the Jetty docs:

  • Produce-Consume (PC): the selector thread runs the task itself. No hand-off and warm CPU caches, but every other socket on that selector waits. The docs say this mode is equivalent to the event loop of Node.js or Netty.
  • Produce-Execute-Consume (PEC): the task goes to the thread pool. No head-of-line blocking, but a hand-off, a queue and cold caches on another core.
  • Execute-Produce-Consume (EPC): the selector thread runs the task, and a reserved thread, one the pool keeps idle and ready, takes over the selecting. Warm caches and no stall.

The choice follows the task's invocation type. A NON_BLOCKING task runs in PC mode. A BLOCKING task runs in EPC mode when a reserved thread is available, and in PEC mode when none is. Jetty's source notes that this strategy used to be called "Eat What You Kill": the hunter eats what it caught. This section's demo reads the mode from each handler's own stack:

default pool, BLOCKING       -> qtp1636182655-25 :: AdaptiveExecutionStrategy.epcRunTask
default pool, NON_BLOCKING   -> qtp2144284609-37 :: AdaptiveExecutionStrategy.pcRunTask
reservedThreads=0, BLOCKING  -> qtp826865256-50 :: no strategy frame: dispatched to the pool
virtual threads, BLOCKING    -> jetty-vt-1 :: VirtualThread.run

Now you can see why the handler's declaration matters. NonBlocking is a promise that lets Jetty run your code on the selector thread, exactly like a Netty event loop. Break the promise with a JDBC call and every connection on that selector stalls; the docs call it a risk of server lock-up. Containers combine their children's types, so one blocking handler anywhere in a handler tree makes the whole tree blocking. That's safe, but it costs the PC fast path.

Compare that with the other servers you know. Netty-based servers, including Vert.x and Quarkus, run every handler in PC mode on the event loop, and offloading is your job. Tomcat's NIO connector watches sockets with a poller and processes requests on its executor threads (200 by default). Jetty sits in between: it chooses per task, from what your handler declares.

code.title: StrategyDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.nio.l07; import org.eclipse.jetty.io.Content; import org.eclipse.jetty.server.Handler; import org.eclipse.jetty.server.Request; import org.eclipse.jetty.server.Response; import org.eclipse.jetty.server.Server; import org.eclipse.jetty.server.ServerConnector; import org.eclipse.jetty.util.Callback; import org.eclipse.jetty.util.VirtualThreads; import org.eclipse.jetty.util.thread.QueuedThreadPool; import java.net.URI; import java.net.http.HttpClient; import java.net.http.HttpRequest; import java.net.http.HttpResponse; import java.util.Arrays; import java.util.List; import java.util.stream.Collectors; /** Which execution-strategy mode ran the handler? Read it from the handler's own stack. */ public class StrategyDemo { static final HttpClient CLIENT = HttpClient.newBuilder().proxy(HttpClient.Builder.NO_PROXY).build(); static String mode() { List<String> methods = Arrays.stream(Thread.currentThread().getStackTrace()) .filter(f -> f.getClassName().contains("AdaptiveExecutionStrategy") || f.getClassName().contains("VirtualThread")) .map(f -> f.getClassName().replaceAll(".*\\.", "") + "." + f.getMethodName()) .collect(Collectors.toList()); String strategy = methods.stream().filter(m -> m.contains("RunTask") && !m.equals("AdaptiveExecutionStrategy.runTask")) .findFirst().orElse(methods.isEmpty() ? "no strategy frame: dispatched to the pool" : methods.get(0)); return Thread.currentThread().getName() + " :: " + strategy; } static Handler handler(boolean nonBlocking) { return nonBlocking ? new Handler.Abstract.NonBlocking() { @Override public boolean handle(Request r, Response s, Callback c) { Content.Sink.write(s, true, mode(), c); return true; } } : new Handler.Abstract() { @Override public boolean handle(Request r, Response s, Callback c) { Content.Sink.write(s, true, mode(), c); return true; } }; } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { for (String setup : List.of("default pool, BLOCKING", "default pool, NON_BLOCKING", "reservedThreads=0, BLOCKING", "virtual threads, BLOCKING")) { QueuedThreadPool pool = new QueuedThreadPool(); if (setup.startsWith("reservedThreads=0")) pool.setReservedThreads(0); if (setup.startsWith("virtual")) pool.setVirtualThreadsExecutor(VirtualThreads.getNamedVirtualThreadsExecutor("jetty-vt-")); Server server = new Server(pool); ServerConnector connector = new ServerConnector(server); connector.setHost("127.0.0.1"); connector.setPort(0); server.addConnector(connector); server.setHandler(handler(setup.endsWith("NON_BLOCKING"))); server.start(); URI uri = URI.create("http://127.0.0.1:" + connector.getLocalPort() + "/"); CLIENT.send(HttpRequest.newBuilder(uri).build(), HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()); // warm up the connection System.out.printf("%-28s -> %s%n", setup, CLIENT.send(HttpRequest.newBuilder(uri).build(), HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()).body()); server.stop(); } } }

Read it from the handler's own stack. */ private val strategyClient = HttpClient.newBuilder().proxy(HttpClient.Builder.NO_PROXY).build() private fun strategyMode(): String { val methods = Thread.currentThread().stackTrace .filter { "AdaptiveExecutionStrategy" in it.className || "VirtualThread" in it.className } .map { it.className.substringAfterLast('.') + "." + it.methodName } val strategy = methods.firstOrNull { "RunTask" in it && it != "AdaptiveExecutionStrategy.runTask" } ?: methods.firstOrNull() ?: "no strategy frame: dispatched to the pool" return "${Thread.currentThread().name} :: $strategy" } private fun modeHandler(nonBlocking: Boolean): Handler = if (nonBlocking) object : Handler.Abstract.NonBlocking() { override fun handle(request: Request, response: Response, callback: Callback): Boolean { Content.Sink.write(response, true, strategyMode(), callback); return true } } else object : Handler.Abstract() { override fun handle(request: Request, response: Response, callback: Callback): Boolean { Content.Sink.write(response, true, strategyMode(), callback); return true } } fun main() { for (setup in listOf("default pool, BLOCKING", "default pool, NON_BLOCKING", "reservedThreads=0, BLOCKING", "virtual threads, BLOCKING")) { val pool = QueuedThreadPool() if (setup.startsWith("reservedThreads=0")) pool.reservedThreads = 0 if (setup.startsWith("virtual")) pool.virtualThreadsExecutor = VirtualThreads.getNamedVirtualThreadsExecutor("jetty-vt-") val server = Server(pool) val connector = ServerConnector(server).apply { host = "127.0.0.1"; port = 0 } server.addConnector(connector) server.handler = modeHandler(setup.endsWith("NON_BLOCKING")) server.start() val uri = URI.create("http://127.0.0.1:${connector.localPort}/") strategyClient.send(HttpRequest.newBuilder(uri).build(), HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()) // warm up the connection println("%-28s -> %s".format(setup, strategyClient.send(HttpRequest.newBuilder(uri).build(), HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()).body())) server.stop() } }

try.expect: Blocking on the default pool: epcRunTask. Non-blocking: pcRunTask, on the selector's own thread. With no reserved threads, a blocking task can't use EPC, because nobody could take over selecting, so it is dispatched to the pool and the handler's stack has no strategy frame at all (PEC). With virtual threads, the PEC path hands the task to a virtual thread, jetty-vt-1.

sections.html:
Jetty 12 offers virtual threads in two ways, and they behave very differently.

The first keeps the QueuedThreadPool and gives it a virtual threads executor:

Java
QueuedThreadPool pool = new QueuedThreadPool(12);
pool.setVirtualThreadsExecutor(VirtualThreads.getNamedVirtualThreadsExecutor("ledger-vt-"));
Kotlin
val pool = QueuedThreadPool(12)
pool.virtualThreadsExecutor = VirtualThreads.getNamedVirtualThreadsExecutor("ledger-vt-")

When the strategy picks PEC for a blocking task, it sends the task to a virtual thread instead of a pool thread. Turning this on sets the reserved threads to zero by default, so blocking tasks always take that path. Acceptors, selectors and non-blocking tasks stay on platform threads. The demo in the first section showed it: the blocking handler ran on jetty-vt-0 and the non-blocking one on a qtp thread.

The second is VirtualThreadPool, which replaces the pool. Despite its name, it doesn't pool virtual threads. It starts a new virtual thread for each task and limits how many tasks run at once with a semaphore, 200 permits by default. With it there are no qtp threads at all: the acceptor and the selectors run on it too.

This section's demo sends 40 concurrent requests to a handler that blocks for 300 ms:

QueuedThreadPool(max=12)               40 x 300 ms -> 1,681 ms, at most 10 in the handler at once
QueuedThreadPool(max=12) + virtual     40 x 300 ms ->   326 ms, at most 40 in the handler at once
VirtualThreadPool(maxThreads=8)        40 x 300 ms -> 2,122 ms, at most 7 in the handler at once

Twelve platform threads minus the leased ones left about ten for requests. The virtual executor let all 40 wait at once. The VirtualThreadPool with 8 permits was slowest, because its permits cap concurrency below even the platform pool, and only 7 ever reached the handler at once, so at least one permit was held by something else at the time.

One version note from the Jetty docs. Jetty dedicates a thread to each Selector, and up to Java 23, calling Selector.select() from a virtual thread pins its carrier; from Java 24 it doesn't. On 21 to 23, then, a server running everything on virtual threads loses one carrier per selector. That is one more reason to prefer the first option: QueuedThreadPool plus the virtual threads executor keeps selectors on platform threads and runs only your blocking handlers virtually. And as in every lesson of this track, virtual threads don't protect your downstream: 40 handlers at once means 40 JDBC calls at once.

import org.eclipse.jetty.server.ServerConnector; import org.eclipse.jetty.util.Callback; import org.eclipse.jetty.util.VirtualThreads; import org.eclipse.jetty.util.thread.QueuedThreadPool; import org.eclipse.jetty.util.thread.ThreadPool; import org.eclipse.jetty.util.thread.VirtualThreadPool; import java.net.URI; import java.net.http.HttpClient; import java.net.http.HttpRequest; import java.net.http.HttpResponse; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; /** 40 concurrent requests to a handler that blocks 300 ms, on three kinds of thread pool. */ public class JettyLoadDemo { static final HttpClient CLIENT = HttpClient.newBuilder() .proxy(HttpClient.Builder.NO_PROXY).version(HttpClient.Version.HTTP_1_1).build(); static class SlowLedger extends Handler.Abstract { final AtomicInteger inFlight = new AtomicInteger(), max = new AtomicInteger(); @Override public boolean handle(Request req, Response res, Callback cb) throws Exception { max.accumulateAndGet(inFlight.incrementAndGet(), Math::max); try { Thread.sleep(300); // the "JDBC call" } finally { inFlight.decrementAndGet(); } Content.Sink.write(res, true, "ok", cb); return true; } } static void run(String label, ThreadPool pool) throws Exception { SlowLedger ledger = new SlowLedger(); Server server = new Server(pool); ServerConnector connector = new ServerConnector(server); connector.setHost("127.0.0.1"); connector.setPort(0); server.addConnector(connector); server.setHandler(ledger); server.start(); URI uri = URI.create("http://127.0.0.1:" + connector.getLocalPort() + "/"); long t0 = System.nanoTime(); List<CompletableFuture<HttpResponse<String>>> calls = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < 40; i++) calls.add(CLIENT.sendAsync(HttpRequest.newBuilder(uri).build(), HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString())); for (var call : calls) call.get(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS); System.out.printf("%-38s 40 x 300 ms -> %,5d ms, at most %d in the handler at once%n", label, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, ledger.max.get()); server.stop(); } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { run("QueuedThreadPool(max=12)", new QueuedThreadPool(12)); QueuedThreadPool withVirtual = new QueuedThreadPool(12); withVirtual.setVirtualThreadsExecutor(VirtualThreads.getNamedVirtualThreadsExecutor("jetty-vt-")); run("QueuedThreadPool(max=12) + virtual", withVirtual); run("VirtualThreadPool(maxThreads=8)", new VirtualThreadPool(8)); } }

alt.title: JettyLoadDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.nio.l07 import org.eclipse.jetty.io.Content import org.eclipse.jetty.server.Handler import org.eclipse.jetty.server.Request import org.eclipse.jetty.server.Response import org.eclipse.jetty.server.Server import org.eclipse.jetty.server.ServerConnector import org.eclipse.jetty.util.Callback import org.eclipse.jetty.util.VirtualThreads import org.eclipse.jetty.util.thread.QueuedThreadPool import org.eclipse.jetty.util.thread.ThreadPool import org.eclipse.jetty.util.thread.VirtualThreadPool import java.net.URI import java.net.http.HttpClient import java.net.http.HttpRequest import java.net.http.HttpResponse import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger /** 40 concurrent requests to a handler that blocks 300 ms, on three kinds of thread pool. */ private val loadClient = HttpClient.newBuilder().proxy(HttpClient.Builder.NO_PROXY).version(HttpClient.Version.HTTP_1_1).build() private class KtSlowLedger : Handler.Abstract() { val inFlight = AtomicInteger() val max = AtomicInteger() override fun handle(request: Request, response: Response, callback: Callback): Boolean { max.accumulateAndGet(inFlight.incrementAndGet()) { a, b -> maxOf(a, b) } try { Thread.sleep(300) // the "JDBC call" } finally { inFlight.decrementAndGet() } Content.Sink.write(response, true, "ok", callback) return true } } private fun runLoad(label: String, pool: ThreadPool) { val ledger = KtSlowLedger() val server = Server(pool) val connector = ServerConnector(server).apply { host = "127.0.0.1"; port = 0 } server.addConnector(connector) server.handler = ledger server.start() val uri = URI.create("http://127.0.0.1:${connector.localPort}/") val t0 = System.nanoTime() val calls = List(40) { loadClient.sendAsync(HttpRequest.newBuilder(uri).build(), HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()) } calls.forEach { it.get(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS) } println("%-38s 40 x 300 ms -> %,5d ms, at most %d in the handler at once".format(label, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, ledger.max.get())) server.stop() } fun main() { runLoad("QueuedThreadPool(max=12)", QueuedThreadPool(12)) val withVirtual = QueuedThreadPool(12) withVirtual.virtualThreadsExecutor = VirtualThreads.getNamedVirtualThreadsExecutor("jetty-vt-") runLoad("QueuedThreadPool(max=12) + virtual", withVirtual) runLoad("VirtualThreadPool(maxThreads=8)", VirtualThreadPool(8)) }

try.expect: About 1.7 s with at most 9 or 10 at once on the 12-thread pool (four rounds of about ten requests), about 330 ms with all 40 at once with the virtual executor, and about 2.1 s with at most 7 at once on VirtualThreadPool(8) (this track's research measured 2.6 to 2.8 s, 0.53 s and 3.0 s for 500 ms requests). With 64 permits, the virtual pool lets all 40 requests run at once and finishes in about the same time as the virtual executor.

analogy: Jetty's adaptive strategy is a chef who also receives the deliveries. When a delivery arrives, the quickest thing is to cook it at once, while the ingredients are still warm, which is Produce-Consume. If the dish takes long (a blocking task), the chef first waves over a standby cook to take over receiving deliveries, then cooks: Execute-Produce-Consume. With no standby cook free, the order goes onto the kitchen's ticket rail for whoever is free next: Produce-Execute-Consume. The analogy breaks where Jetty trusts the order slip: a dish marked "quick" (NonBlocking) is always cooked at the door, even if it turns out to take an hour, and then nobody receives deliveries.
world: You may run Jetty without choosing it: as the embedded server in a service, inside a test harness such as WireMock, or behind a framework. For a payments team the useful knobs are few. Declare honestly whether your handlers block. Size the QueuedThreadPool as leased threads plus request threads, and never give it a bounded queue. Use a QoS handler to shed load, not the pool. On JDK 21 or newer, turn on the virtual threads executor for a blocking service, and keep a real limit (the JDBC pool, a semaphore) in front of the database and the card issuer, because Jetty will now happily run 2,000 handlers at once.
mistake: The most damaging mistake is extending Handler.Abstract.NonBlocking because it sounds faster, then calling JDBC, a synchronous HTTP client or anything else that waits. The superclass is a promise: Jetty runs the handler on the selector thread in Produce-Consume mode, so every other connection on that selector waits behind your query, which is the event-loop failure from lessons 3 and 5. Extend Handler.Abstract for anything that might block. A close second is giving the QueuedThreadPool a bounded queue to protect the server: the docs say the queue must be unbounded, because Jetty's own progress depends on tasks that must not be rejected.

compare.title: An asynchronous echo handler in Java and Kotlin

java.title: EchoHandler.java
java.html: public class EchoHandler extends Handler.Abstract.NonBlocking { @Override public boolean handle(Request request, Response response, Callback callback) { Content.Source.asStringAsync(request, UTF_8).whenComplete((body, failure) -> { if (failure != null) { Response.writeError(request, response, callback, failure); return; } Content.Sink.write(response, true, "echo: " + body, callback); // completes the callback }); return true; // "I took this request"; the response finishes later } }

kotlin.title: EchoHandler.kt
kotlin.html: class EchoHandler : Handler.Abstract.NonBlocking() { override fun handle(request: Request, response: Response, callback: Callback): Boolean { Content.Source.asStringAsync(request, UTF_8).whenComplete { body, failure -> if (failure != null) { Response.writeError(request, response, callback, failure) } else { Content.Sink.write(response, true, "echo: $body", callback) // completes the callback } } return true // "I took this request"; the response finishes later } }

compare.note: The two are the same handler at runtime. The Kotlin version shows two small differences. The BiConsumer passed to whenComplete becomes a two-parameter lambda, and if/else replaces the early return, because a bare return inside a Kotlin lambda would return from handle itself and doesn't compile here (you'd need return@whenComplete). Kotlin also lets you write Jetty's setters as properties (server.handler = ..., pool.virtualThreadsExecutor = ...). The threading is identical: the lambda runs on whichever thread completes the body future, which can be a different thread from the one that called handle.

worked.title: Move a blocking ledger service onto virtual threads

steps.say: A Jetty service serves balances with a 300 ms JDBC query per request on a pool of 50. Under a burst of 400 requests the tail latency explodes. Little's law: about 45 threads can run handlers, so 400 requests need 400 / 45 × 0.3 s, about 2.7 s, to drain, while the CPU is nearly idle.
steps.code: QueuedThreadPool pool = new QueuedThreadPool(50); // about 45 left after leasing Server server = new Server(pool); server.setHandler(new LedgerHandler(300));

alt.html: val pool = QueuedThreadPool(50) // about 45 left after leasing val server = Server(pool) server.handler = LedgerHandler(300)

steps.say: Keep the handler and give blocking tasks virtual threads. The pool keeps its platform threads for acceptors and selectors; every blocking handler gets a virtual thread, so the burst no longer queues for threads.
steps.code: QueuedThreadPool pool = new QueuedThreadPool(50); pool.setVirtualThreadsExecutor(VirtualThreads.getNamedVirtualThreadsExecutor("ledger-vt-"));

alt.html: val pool = QueuedThreadPool(50) pool.virtualThreadsExecutor = VirtualThreads.getNamedVirtualThreadsExecutor("ledger-vt-")

steps.say: Now the queue has moved to the database. 400 handlers all ask the connection pool, which has 20 connections. That is the right place for the wait, but give it a timeout, so a slow database turns into fast errors instead of 400 stuck requests.
steps.code: HikariConfig config = new HikariConfig(); config.setMaximumPoolSize(20); // the real concurrency limit config.setConnectionTimeout(500); // ms to wait for a connection, then fail

alt.html: val config = HikariConfig().apply { maximumPoolSize = 20 // the real concurrency limit connectionTimeout = 500 // ms to wait for a connection, then fail }

steps.say: Check the health endpoint is still cheap. It extends Handler.Abstract.NonBlocking, so it keeps running on platform threads in Produce-Consume mode, which the lab's last test asserts. If someone later adds a database ping to it, change its superclass in the same commit.

lab.title: Build Jetty core handlers and move blocking ones to virtual threads
steps: Run the tests. All five fail.

Fix StatusHandler's superclass so it declares itself non-blocking. Write LedgerHandler.serve: sleep delayMs, write the body from its Javadoc with Content.Sink.write, return true. The invocation-type test should pass.
Write PaymentServer.start: new Server(pool), a ServerConnector on host 127.0.0.1 and port 0, setHandler, start(). The platform-pool test should pass: read its assertion on maxConcurrent().
Write EchoHandler.handle with Content.Source.asStringAsync and return true right away.
Write PaymentServer.virtualQueuedThreadPool. Run all five tests. The last one shows that StatusHandler stays on platform threads even with virtual threads enabled.
hints: Thread.currentThread().isVirtual() gives the virtual= part of the ledger body.
If the echo test hangs and then fails, check that every path through the whenComplete lambda completes the callback, either with Content.Sink.write(..., callback) or with Response.writeError(...).
With QueuedThreadPool(12) the connector leases one acceptor and one selector thread, and one more is kept as a reserved thread, so fewer than 12 handlers ever run at once.
If the last test fails with virtual=true, StatusHandler still extends Handler.Abstract, so Jetty treats it as blocking and sends it to a virtual thread.

drill.title: Write an asynchronous Jetty handler from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. Write a Jetty 12 core handler that reads the whole request body without blocking and answers echo: <body>. Which superclass, what does handle return, and who completes the callback?

answer.html: public class EchoHandler extends Handler.Abstract.NonBlocking { @Override public boolean handle(Request request, Response response, Callback callback) { Content.Source.asStringAsync(request, UTF_8).whenComplete((body, failure) -> { if (failure != null) { Response.writeError(request, response, callback, failure); return; } Content.Sink.write(response, true, "echo: " + body, callback); // completes the callback }); return true; // "I took this request"; the response finishes later } } // Superclass: Handler.Abstract.NonBlocking (it never blocks). // handle returns true at once; Content.Sink.write or Response.writeError completes the callback later.

alt.html: class EchoHandler : Handler.Abstract.NonBlocking() { override fun handle(request: Request, response: Response, callback: Callback): Boolean { Content.Source.asStringAsync(request, UTF_8).whenComplete { body, failure -> if (failure != null) { Response.writeError(request, response, callback, failure) } else { Content.Sink.write(response, true, "echo: $body", callback) // completes the callback } } return true // "I took this request"; the response finishes later } } // Superclass: Handler.Abstract.NonBlocking (it never blocks). // handle returns true at once; Content.Sink.write or Response.writeError completes the callback later.

recap: A Jetty Server links connectors and handlers to one ThreadPool. A ServerConnector runs acceptors (1 by default) and ManagedSelectors, one thread each, max(1, min(cpus / 2, maxThreads / 16)) by default.
QueuedThreadPool defaults to 8 to 200 threads; connectors lease some for good, and its queue must stay unbounded. Shed load with a QoS handler.

The core API is boolean handle(Request, Response, Callback): return true and complete the callback exactly once, maybe later. Read bodies as Content.Source chunks and release them, or use helpers like asStringAsync.
AdaptiveExecutionStrategy runs NON_BLOCKING tasks on the selector thread (PC), BLOCKING ones on the selector thread with a reserved thread taking over (EPC), or hands them off (PEC).

setVirtualThreadsExecutor sends only blocking tasks to virtual threads; VirtualThreadPool runs everything virtually and caps tasks with a semaphore. Before Java 24, selectors on virtual threads pin carriers.
Netty-based servers always run handlers on the event loop; Tomcat runs requests on executor threads; Jetty chooses per task from what the handler declares.

explain.prompt: A colleague says "Jetty is just a thread-per-request server like Tomcat". Explain what Jetty 12 actually does between reading a socket and calling a handler, and why a handler's superclass matters.
explain.answer: A Jetty connector has an acceptor thread that accepts sockets and selector threads, each running a java.nio select loop. When a selector sees a readable connection, it produces a task that parses the request and calls the handler, and the adaptive execution strategy decides who runs that task. If the handler declares itself non-blocking (Handler.Abstract.NonBlocking), the selector thread runs it directly, like an event loop, with no hand-off. If it declares itself blocking (Handler.Abstract), the selector thread still runs it when a reserved thread is free to take over selecting, which keeps caches warm; otherwise the task goes to the thread pool, or to a virtual thread if that executor is configured. So Jetty is neither purely thread-per-request nor purely an event loop: it chooses per task, based on the declaration. That's why the superclass matters. A handler that claims to be non-blocking and then calls JDBC stalls every connection on its selector, while an honest blocking declaration costs at most a thread hand-off.

deeper.html:
Three details from the Jetty 12.1 sources and docs round out the picture.

There is a fourth mode. AdaptiveExecutionStrategy's Javadoc names Produce-Invoke-Consume for tasks whose invocation type is EITHER: they are run with Invocable.invokeNonBlocking, meaning the task is asked to proceed in a non-blocking way if it can. The selection order is PC for a non-blocking task, EPC if a reserved thread is available, PIC for EITHER, and PEC otherwise. Strategies also nest: the selector's strategy produces connection tasks, and an HTTP/2 connection runs its own strategy over its streams.

Jetty also has the reverse problem of a declared handler. Request.demand(Runnable), which asks Jetty to call you back when more body content is available, treats a plain lambda as blocking. If your callback really is non-blocking, pass an Invocable.Task that declares so, or Jetty may hand it off to another thread for nothing.

On sizing: each connector leases a thread per acceptor and per selector, and ReservedThreadExecutor leases its reserved threads, by default max(1, ceilToNextPowerOfTwo(min(cpus, maxThreads / 8))), or 0 once a virtual threads executor is set. The docs suggest maxThreads = leased threads + threads you want for handlers, and remind you that idle threads shrink back according to idleTimeout. Raising maxThreads to thousands is the old fix for blocking handlers; on JDK 21 or newer, the virtual threads executor is the cheaper one.

HTTP/3 shows how far the connector abstraction stretches: Jetty implements HTTP/3 in Java but uses the native Quiche library for QUIC, through JNA, with a connector that has zero acceptors and a single selector over a DatagramChannel.
